key_concepts.definition: Broader game category encompassing video games and electronic games without video output.
Electronic game involving player interaction that affects a visual display; a winning condition is not mandatory.
Participant who interacts with a game; participation can include controlling an avatar or limited setup followed by observation.
Activity through which a player interacts with a game; video-game-defining interactivity affects its visual display.
Visual information produced by a game, including fixed-display, text-based, two-dimensional, three-dimensional and augmented reality forms.
Victory criterion, such as a scoring mechanism or final boss fight, present in most but not all video games.
Interactive world provided by a game, including games without winning conditions.
Progression division found in most games, through which a player works an avatar.
In-game representation worked through levels by the player in the described gameplay.
Innate property of an avatar that a power-up can boost.
Avatar property depleted by damage; reaching zero triggers loss of a life in the described gameplay.
Countable gameplay allowance lost under the described failure conditions; an Extra Life, also called 1-UP, adds a life.
Collectible that can boost an avatar’s innate attributes.
Gameplay occurrence that depletes an avatar’s health.
Recorded game state or re-enterable passage allowing a game to restart after lost lives or interrupted play.
On-screen user interface presenting gameplay information over the rendered game.
Combination of electronic components or computer hardware and associated software required to operate a game; also called a system.
Electronic components or computer hardware forming a platform’s physical computing facilities.
Programs associated with a platform and operation of its games.
Original game program material reused to a substantial extent in a remaster.
Game developed for a platform other than originally intended; also called a conversion.
Derived game reusing most original source code while updating art assets, models and levels for modern systems.
Derived game involving asset improvements and significant reworking of the original, possibly from scratch.
Portable, self-contained console integrating a small screen, speakers and controls in one unit.
Device such as a smartphone or tablet whose features may support augmented reality gameplay.
Game computed and rendered on remote hardware supplied by a cloud gaming provider.
Game generally using a head-mounted unit with stereoscopic screens and motion tracking.
Head-worn VR equipment providing stereoscopic screens and motion tracking.
Software enabling another system’s games to run on a modern system by simulating original hardware in a virtual machine.
Simulated execution environment in which an emulator reproduces original-system hardware for games.
Platform capability to play older games, typically directly through newer hardware and built-in software.
Physical formats used to distribute games, including ROM cartridges, magnetic storage, optical media and flash memory cards.
Game extension providing new content and software patches, typically available as physical media.
Game extension providing new content and software patches, nominally available through digital distribution.
Player-created alteration or addition to a game, also called a mod; often unofficial, although official support can exist.
Participant in the collaboration that brings a game to consumers, with development, publishing, distribution, retail, hardware or marketing roles.
Party involved in bringing a game to consumers and able to submit a content-rating review.
Device translating human actions into game input.
Input device used to control games, including general-purpose and specialized controllers.
Device presenting game graphics, such as a television, built-in screen, projector or computer monitor.
Technology providing tactile feedback, such as shaking a controller in a player’s hands.
Game grouping generally based on gameplay interaction; the document also describes subgenres, cross-genre types and a narrative-based horror exception.
Description of simultaneous player participation, primarily single-player or multiplayer; the document also identifies zero-player games.
Number of players able to use a game at the same time.
Entertainment-oriented game, also called hard-core, typically requiring a fair amount of time to learn and master.
Game designed for accessibility, simple-to-understand gameplay and quickly grasped rule sets.
Game designed to teach, broadly divided in the document into edutainment games and problem-solving-oriented educational video games.
The document’s narrower educational branch emphasizing problem solving, motivation and positive reinforcement while downplaying entertainment.
Game whose non-entertainment purposes may augment, overshadow or eliminate its entertainment factor.
Game designed to generate player emotion and empathy through interactive artistic expression; also called an arthouse game.
Assessment of age appropriateness informed by content such as violence, sexual content, drug or alcohol use, and gambling.
Rating scheme generally using a primary minimum-age identifier and content descriptors, with practices and regulation varying by country.
Body that oversees or assigns game content ratings in a national or regional context.
Provider with which a publisher completes a content-rating review in the IARC process.
Primary rating identifier based on the minimum age considered appropriate for the player.
Additional rating information identifying specific content that players and parents should know about.
Geographic scope within which a rating organization or system operates.
Entertainment Software Rating Board, described as overseeing games released in the United States.
Pan European Game Information, the named rating system covering the United Kingdom, most of the European Union and other European countries.
Australian Classification Board, described as overseeing ratings of games and other works in Australia.
Computer Entertainment Rating Organization, described as rating games for Japan.
Unterhaltungssoftware Selbstkontrolle, described as rating games for Germany.
International Age Rating Coalition, supporting affirmation of content ratings across regions after review with one provider.

assumptions: The explicit instruction not to impose a fixed concept or relationship maximum takes precedence over the earlier 12-entry schema caption.
The supplied 50 CQs determine coverage; expected answers and ODP hints guide requirements but do not independently establish source facts.
This is a document-grounded model. Platform and regional rating statements are retained as described, not presented as independently verified current facts.

key_concepts identifies core abstractions rather than an exhaustive vocabulary. Taxonomy endpoints not separately defined remain reusable Category terms; named geographic places denote entities and unenumerated regional expressions retain their textual scope.

Generic relationships and activity entries describe reusable patterns rather than universal instance assertions or identified event occurrences. Repeated Party participants denote role-fillers whose identities and possible overlap are unspecified.
Qualifiers preserve most, many, typically, generally, may and the described-gameplay scope; these do not become universal restrictions, exact maxima or guaranteed outcomes.

Platform groupings, derivative-version forms and participation modes are represented relationally, not as subclasses. No disjointness, exclusivity or mandatory possession of every listed option is inferred.
Temporal content is restricted to CQ-relevant relative gameplay conditions and qualitative learning duration. Unrequested historical dates, market figures and named-game examples are omitted.
Citation markers annotate prose for provenance and are not ontology terms, predicates or identifiers.
